_about: Analyst question bank (12 Nov 2026). The finance team owns this file: edit the questions here, not in code.

Rules: (1) general rules only, never about one company or ticker; (2) NO DIGITS in any question text: the number guardrail treats every figure the AI reads as quotable data, so write 'half', 'five to ten years', 'its own history' instead of numbers; (3) short, plain questions a first-year student can read.

general = asked for every company. sectors = asked only when the company's sector / industry name (Yahoo or EastMoney) contains one of the lower-case `match` words; the first sector that matches wins, so put specific sectors before broad ones. A sector with financial: true is used for banks and insurers (quant/valuation.is_financial), whatever its words.

Fields per question: id (stable, lower_case, unique in the whole file), theme (one of `themes`), text, and optionally: data = the key of a figure computed in code (narrative/questions.py COMPUTE); look = the report chapter to point the reader to (overview, financials, statements, valuation, street, competitive, technical, news, ownership, filings); core: true = always asked when the code chooses (the data-only edition); skip_financial: true = not asked for banks and insurers.

Every report shows a selection: the AI picks the most relevant (at most eight) and may add up to three new company-specific questions from recent evidence; the data-only edition shows the code's choice (core questions, sector questions, then questions with figures).

general.text: What is the moat, in one sentence: brand, switching costs, network effects, scale or regulation?
Is the moat widening or narrowing over the next five to ten years?
What would make this business earn half as much in a decade?
Does the company have pricing power, or is its gross margin being squeezed?
Could the balance sheet carry the company through a bad year?
Who are the real competitors, including non-obvious ones and substitutes?
What shift in technology, rules or customer habits could make the business model obsolete?
How cyclical is demand: is this a structural grower, a steady compounder or a cyclical?
How much operating leverage is there: do profits swing more than sales?
Is the company a price-maker or a price-taker in its industry?
Is revenue spread out, or concentrated in a few customers, products or regions?
Does profit turn into cash (operating cash flow against net profit)?
Do 'one-off' costs or gains keep coming back, and how much profit comes from outside operations?
Are receivables growing faster than revenue?
Is the share count really falling once stock-based pay is set against buybacks?
Does management reinvest at returns above the cost of capital?
Where does the cash go (reinvestment, acquisitions, dividends, buybacks), and are shares bought back only when they are cheap?
Has management met the targets it set in the past?
Is management's pay tied to long-term value per share?
Is the auditor's report clean, with no qualification and no recent change of auditor?
What drives growth: volume, price, new markets or operating leverage?
Is growth organic, or bought through acquisitions?
What do we believe that the consensus does not?
How long is the runway to keep reinvesting at high returns?
What growth does today's price imply (reverse DCF), and is that realistic?
Is there a margin of safety between the price and a sober estimate of value?
Is the stock cheap or dear against its own history and its peers?
What could close the gap between price and value, and when?
What is the bear case, and which data we can observe would show it unfolding?

questions.text: Does return on equity stay above the cost of equity through the cycle?
How good is the loan book: are bad loans and provisions rising?
How sensitive is the interest margin to changes in interest rates?
Is capital strong enough to keep paying dividends while the balance sheet grows?
Is the price-to-book ratio justified by the returns?
Is funding stable: customer deposits or wholesale borrowing?
Where is the concentrated exposure: property, one region or one industry?
What return does the regulator allow, and when is it next reset?
How is the investment plan funded: debt, new shares or cash flow?
Can the balance sheet carry more debt if interest rates rise?
Is the dividend growing in line with the regulated asset base?
How exposed is the company to fuel costs, weather and wholesale power prices?
What commodity price does the company need to cover its costs and its dividend?
How long can production last at the current reserves?
Is investment in new projects disciplined, or chasing growth at the top of the cycle?
How exposed is the business to the energy transition and climate rules?
Is the dividend covered by free cash flow at mid-cycle prices?
How strong is the balance sheet if commodity prices fall?
What are occupancy and rents doing, and how long are the leases?
How much debt falls due soon, and at what cost can it be refinanced?
Is the share price below or above the value of the properties?
Are sales and cash collections keeping up with construction costs?
Is the dividend paid from recurring cash flow?
How exposed is the company to one city or one type of property?
When do the key patents expire, and what replaces the lost sales?
How strong is the pipeline, and which trial results or approvals are due next?
How much do drug-pricing rules and reimbursement threaten margins?
How much of revenue rests on a few products?
Is research turning into new products?
Is the company facing legal, safety or regulatory cases?
Where are crop or livestock prices in their cycle, and how do they move profits?
How exposed is the company to weather, disease and harvest swings?
Is the company squeezed between feed or input costs and its selling prices?
How do trade policy, tariffs and subsidies affect demand and prices?
Are inventories of crops or livestock valued conservatively?
Does it own land, seeds or brands that give it pricing power, or is it a price-taker?
How much of revenue depends on a few large customers, and how much do they plan to invest?
Where are we in the chip cycle: are inventories building at the company or its customers?
Can supply (foundry capacity, advanced packaging, memory) keep up with demand?
How exposed is revenue to export controls and geopolitics?
Is the product lead secure for the next generations, or can rivals and customers' own chips catch up?
Is research and development keeping pace with revenue and with rivals?
How dependent is the company on one flagship product or one large customer?
Does it own the software, services or ecosystem that keep customers coming back?
Are component costs and supply under control?
Are inventories rising faster than sales?
How fast do products age, and where is the replacement cycle now?
How much of manufacturing depends on one country or one contract manufacturer?
Are users and engagement still growing, or is growth now coming from price?
How much revenue depends on advertising, and how sensitive is it to the economy?
What does a new customer cost to win, and how long do customers stay?
Are privacy, competition or content rules a threat to the model?
Is stock-based pay a large hidden cost?
Is the investment in data centres and AI earning a return?
Can the brand raise prices faster than costs without losing volume?
Is growth coming from volume, price or a richer product mix?
Is stock building up at distributors and flattering sales?
Are private labels or new brands taking shelf space?
How exposed is the company to raw-material and packaging costs?
Is the dividend safely covered by free cash flow?
Are prices holding, or is the company buying volume with discounts?
How is the shift to electric cars and software changing its profits?
Does it have the scale to fund new models and plants?
How much depends on one market, and how exposed is it to tariffs?
What are the warranty, recall and pension risks?
Is the car-finance arm adding risk to the balance sheet?
Is capacity being added faster than demand?
How exposed are margins to lithium and other raw-material prices?
How concentrated are customers among a few car makers?
Is the technology and cost lead holding against rivals?
How much do subsidies, tariffs and trade rules shape demand?
Are receivables and inventories growing faster than sales?
